verses.zh: 耶和华要怜恤雅各，必再拣选以色列，将他们安置在本地。寄居的必与他们联合，紧贴雅各家。
verses.en: The Lord will certainly have compassion on Jacob;[NOTE:1] he will again choose Israel as his special people[NOTE:2] and restore[NOTE:3] them to their land. Resident foreigners will join them and unite with the family[NOTE:4] of Jacob.
notes: The sentence begins with כִּי (ki), which is understood as asseverative (“certainly”) in the translation. Another option is to translate, “For the Lord will have compassion.” In this case one of the reasons for Babylon’s coming demise (13:22b) is the Lord’s desire to restore his people.
The words “as his special people” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
Or “settle” (NASB, NIV, NCV, NLT).
Heb “house.”
verses.commentary:
14:1 "the Lord will have compassion" This VERB
(BDB 933, KB 1216, Piel IMPERFECT, cf. Isa. 49:13,15; 54:7-8) denotes YHWH's
special relationship with His covenant people (cf. Hosea 1-2; 11:8-11). This special relationship is also seen in
the VERB "choose" (BDB 103, KB 119, Qal PERFECT with waw,
cf. Isa. 41:8,9; 44:1; 49:7). In Isa. 9:17 Israel's God will have no compassion on His covenant people
and in Isa. 13:18 the Medes will have no compassion on Old Babylon, but YHWH will again
restore His unique relationship with Abraham's seed!

After YHWH uses the powers of Mesopotamia to punish His covenant people's disobedience,
He will instigate a "new exodus."

SPECIAL TOPIC: HE CHOSE US

▣ "Jacob. . .Israel" These two terms could be used for both the Northern Ten Tribes and the Southern
Two Tribes being united again.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

14:1-2 There are two options for interpreting Isa. 14:1-2:

- either Isa. 14:1 and 2 go together and describe the same group (i.e. strangers. . .peoples)

- or Isa. 14:1 describes the blessings of non-Jews (i.e. strangers) and Isa. 14:2 describes the
defeated enemies of Israel as being their servants

It is difficult in Isaiah and Micah to balance YHWH's attitude and actions towards
the nations.

- He loves them and includes them into His covenant people (cf. Isa. 2:2-4; 11:10, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

- He judges them and puts them in servitude (i.e. Isa. 60:10; 61:5)

Somehow both are true! The prophets move back and forth, often in the same context, between
these two poles. Option #1 reflects Genesis 1-3; 12:3, while option #2 reflects Israel's history in Canaan.

In Isaiah the nations return the covenant people to their land (i.e. Canaan) and become one
with them in the worship of YHWH (cf. Isa. 49:22; 60:4-9,10-14; 66:20). This may reflect the "new exodus."
Many foreign people left Egypt with Israel and others joined her along the way (wilderness wanderings and
conquest). Maybe the imagery of Isa. 14:2 reflects this. If so, it would solve the problem of #2 above.

verses.zh: 外邦人必将他们带回本土；以色列家必在耶和华的地上得外邦人为仆婢，也要掳掠先前掳掠他们的，辖制先前欺压他们的。
verses.en: Nations will take them and bring them back to their own place. Then the family of Israel will make foreigners their servants as they settle in the Lord’s land.[NOTE:1] They will make their captors captives and rule over the ones who oppressed them.
notes: Heb “and the house of Israel will take possession of them [i.e., the nations], on the land of the Lord, as male servants and female servants.”
verses.commentary:
14:2-3 There is a "role-reversal" between Isa. 14:2 (servitude of Israel's enemies) and Isa. 14:3
(Israel's servitude, which is now over). The "role-reversal" plot is common in the OT. YHWH acts in
unexpected ways to affirm the choice of Abraham's seed (cf. Genesis 12; 15; 17). The purpose of His
special attention is not favoritism, but an eternal redemptive plan (cf. Gen. 3:15; 12:3) for all
humans made in His image (cf. Gen. 1:26-27).

As so often in Isaiah, there is a short-term focus and a long-term focus. The prophet merges
these two horizons. A good example might be chapter 13, where old Babylon and Neo-Babylon's judgment are merged.

verses.zh: 当耶和华使你脱离愁苦、烦恼，并人勉强你做的苦工，得享安息的日子，
verses.en: When the Lord gives you relief from your suffering and anxiety[NOTE:1] and from the hard labor that you were made to perform,
notes: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.

verses.zh: 你必题这诗歌论巴比伦王说：欺压人的何竟息灭？强暴的何竟止息？
verses.en: you will taunt the king of Babylon with these words:[NOTE:1] “Look how the oppressor has met his end!Hostility[NOTE:2] has ceased!
notes: Heb “you will lift up this taunt over the king of Babylon, saying.”

The word in the Hebrew text (מַדְהֵבָה, madhevah) is unattested elsewhere and of uncertain meaning. Many (following the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa) assume a confusion of dalet and resh (ד and ר) and emend the form to מַרְהֵבָה (marhevah, “onslaught”). See HALOT 548 s.v. II *מִדָּה and HALOT 633 s.v. *מַרְהֵבָה.
verses.commentary:
14:4 "taunt" This is the Hebrew Wisdom Literature term mashal (BDB 605), which is
usually translated "proverb." However, the poetic structure of Isa. 14:3-21 is in the meter of a funeral
dirge (i.e. chapter 47 and Lamentations).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WISDOM LITERATURE

▣ "against the king of Babylon" The peson identified by this title is uncertain. Please
read "Contextual Insights," C, second paragraph of chapter 13. Notice how in Isa. 14:24, without any
"oracle" formula, Assyria is addressed directly. After the fall of the city of Babylon to Assyria
in 689 B.C., the Assyrian kings took the added throne title of "king of Babylon."

NASB
"the oppressor has ceased"

NKJV
"the golden city ceased"

NRSV
"his insolence has ceased"

NJB
"how did his arrogance end"

LXX
"the taskmaster has ceased"

JPSOA
"the oppression ended"

Peshitta
"the zealous one ceased"

REB
"how still his raging arrogance"

The MT has the word מדהבה
(BDB 551, from an Aramaic root, cf. NKJV), but this is used only here in the OT. If the
ד (d) is changed to ר (r),
like the scroll of Isaiah in the Dead Sea Scrolls, then
מרהבה (BDB 923) becomes "arrogant" or
"insolent." The UBS Text Project gives this emendation a "C" rating (considerable doubt) rating.

verses.zh: 耶和华折断了恶人的杖，辖制人的圭，
verses.en: The Lord has broken the club of the wicked,the scepter of rulers.
verses.commentary:
14:5 "The Lord has" YHWH is the controller behind human history (cf.
Isa. 14:22-23,24). He may be unseen to those who lack faith, but He is directing history for His coming
of Messiah (first coming inaugurates the Kingdom) and the consummation of the age of righteousness (second coming).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SECOND COMING

SPECIAL TOPIC: THIS AGE AND THE AGE TO COME

SPECIAL TOPIC: MESSIANIC ERA

▣ The "staff" (BDB 641) and "scepter" (BDB 986) were symbols of kingly power (cf. Isa. 14:6). They
are used as imagery of YHWH's use of Assyria as His tool for judgment on His people in Isa. 10:5.

verses.zh: 就是在忿怒中连连攻击众民的，在怒气中辖制列国，行逼迫无人阻止的。
verses.en: It[NOTE:1] furiously struck down nationswith unceasing blows.[NOTE:2] It angrily ruled over nations,oppressing them without restraint.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or perhaps, “he” (cf. KJV; NCV “the king of Babylon”). The present translation understands the referent of the pronoun (“it”) to be the “club/scepter” of the preceding line.
Heb “it was striking down nations in fury [with] a blow without ceasing.” The participle (“striking down”) suggests repeated or continuous action in past time.
Heb “it was ruling in anger nations [with] oppression without restraint.” The participle (“ruling”) suggests repeated or continuous action in past time.

verses.zh: 现在全地得安息，享平静；人皆发声欢呼。
verses.en: The whole earth rests and is quiet;they break into song.
verses.commentary:
14:7 "The whole earth is at rest and is quiet" The "rest" (BDB 628, KB 679, Qal
PERFECT) refers to a time of peace from invasion. This same VERB
is used in Isa. 14:3 (Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) to refer to the rest/peace of the
covenant people. Here it refers to the whole ANE (i.e. "the whole earth"). See
SPECIAL TOPIC: LAND, COUNTRY, EARTH

The fall of the Mesopotamian powers causes rest, quiet, and joy throughout the ANE. The
oppressor is defeated (cf. Isa. 14:8).

▣ "They break forth into shouts of joy" Isaiah speaks often of the joy of deliverance (i.e. salvation, cf.
Isa. 44:23; 49:13; 52:9; 54:1).

Here, it has an element of an eschatological joy (i.e. "the whole earth"). YHWH's will
for mankind was rest, peace, abundance, and joy (cf. Genesis 1-2)!

verses.zh: 松树和黎巴嫩的香柏树都因你欢乐，说：自从你仆倒，再无人上来砍伐我们。
verses.en: The evergreens also rejoice over your demise,[NOTE:1] as do the cedars of Lebanon, singing,[NOTE:2] ‘Since you fell asleep,[NOTE:3] no woodsman comes up to chop us down!’[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “concerning you.”
The word “singing” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. Note that the personified trees speak in the second half of the verse.
Heb “lay down” (in death); cf. NAB “laid to rest.”
Heb “the [wood]cutter does not come up against us.”
verses.commentary:
14:8 "no tree cutter comes up against us" This can mean one of three things.

- Babylon exported many trees from Lebanon for her own building projects (literal)

- the enemy will not cut lumber to build siege equipment (literal)

- the land will prosper in peace (symbolic)

From Assyrian documents we learn cutting timber was common imagery for defeating foreign
armies. In Isa. 10:33-34 this imagery is used of YHWH's action.

verses.zh: 你下到阴间，阴间就因你震动来迎接你，又因你惊动在世曾为首领的阴魂，并使那曾为列国君王的，都离位站起。
verses.en: Sheol[NOTE:1] below is stirred up about you,ready to meet you when you arrive.It rouses[NOTE:2] the spirits of the dead for you,all the former leaders of the earth;[NOTE:3] it makes all the former kings of the nationsrise from their thrones.[NOTE:4]
notes: Sheol is the proper name of the subterranean world which was regarded as the land of the dead.
Heb “arousing.” The form is probably a Polel infinitive absolute, rather than a third masculine singular perfect, for Sheol is grammatically feminine (note “stirred up”). See GKC 466 §145.t.
Heb “all the rams of the earth.” The animal epithet is used metaphorically here for leaders. See HALOT 903 s.v. *עַתּוּד.

Heb “lifting from their thrones all the kings of the nations.” הֵקִים (heqim, a Hiphil perfect third masculine singular) should be emended to an infinitive absolute (הָקֵים, haqem). See the note on “rouses” earlier in the verse.
verses.commentary:
14:9 "Sheol" Sheol is personified as preparing a welcoming gathering for the fallen kings. It (BDB 982)
refers to the holding place of the dead. In the OT life after death is described as being a conscious existence,
but with no joy; people being a mere shadow of their former selves with enforced equality in silence
(cf. Isa. 14:10-11, Job 3:17-19; 10:21-22; 21:23-26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD? I. B.

NASB
"spirits of the dead"

NKJV
"the dead"

NRSV, JPSOA
"the shades"

TEV, NJB
"ghosts"

LXX
"mighty ones"

REB
"the ancient dead"

Peshitta
"mighty men"

The term (BDB 952 I, cf. Isa. 26:19) is used in poetry for

- dead kings, TEV, NJB

- dead warriors, LXX

- dead ancestors, REB

- the dead in general, NASB, NKJV

In historical texts it refers to the Rephaim, an ethnic group associated with the giants. In
Canaanite mythology this term referred to dead kings, leaders, and military heroes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS

NASB, NKJV, REB
"leaders of the earth"

NKJV
"chief one of the earth"

TEV
"those who were powerful"

NJB, Peshitta
"rulers of the world"

JPSOA
"earth's chieftans"

LXX
"who have ruled the earth"

This is literally "rams" (BDB 800, cf. Ezek. 34:17). It referred to the leader of a flock and
then metaphorically of human societies. This is obviously ANE hyperbole, refering to the known world
of that day.

verses.zh: 他们都要发言对你说：你也变为软弱像我们一样吗？你也成了我们的样子吗？
verses.en: All of them respond to you, saying:‘You too have become weak like us!You have become just like us!

verses.zh: 你的威势和你琴瑟的声音都下到阴间。你下铺的是虫，上盖的是蛆。
verses.en: Your splendor[NOTE:1] has been brought down to Sheol,as well as the sound of your stringed instruments.[NOTE:2] You lie on a bed of maggots,with a blanket of worms over you.’[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “pride” (NCV, CEV); KJV, NIV, NRSV “pomp.”
Or “harps” (NAB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “under you maggots are spread out, and worms are your cover.”
verses.commentary:
14:11 The first two lines denote the lavish and extravagant lifestyle of the ANE kings. They lay
on pillows and slept on soft beds.

The last two lines describe the new bed of the kings in Sheol/grave (i.e. worms). Even the
monarchs who saw themselves as gods, will one day be in a bed of worms! Mortality is a leveler of all
mankind (cf. Isa. 5:14). What a contrast!

▣ "worms" Here it is used literally as an idiom for death and imagery for the fear of death
and transitoriness of all human life.

verses.zh: 明亮之星，早晨之子啊，你何竟从天坠落？你这攻败列国的何竟被砍倒在地上？
verses.en: “Look how you have fallen from the sky,O shining one, son of the dawn![NOTE:1] You have been cut down to the ground,O conqueror[NOTE:2] of the nations![NOTE:3]
notes: The Hebrew text has הֵילֵל בֶּן־שָׁחַר (helel ben shakhar, “Helel son of Shachar”), which is probably a name for the morning star (Venus) or the crescent moon. See HALOT 245 s.v. הֵילֵל. sn What is the background for the imagery in vv. 12-15? This whole section (vv. 4b-21) is directed to the king of Babylon, who is clearly depicted as a human ruler. Other kings of the earth address him in vv. 9ff., he is called “the man” in v. 16, and, according to vv. 19-20, he possesses a physical body. Nevertheless the language of vv. 12-15 has led some to see a dual referent in the taunt song. These verses, which appear to be spoken by other pagan kings to a pagan king (cf. vv. 9-11), contain several titles and motifs that resemble those of Canaanite mythology, including references to Helel son of Shachar, the stars of El, the mountain of assembly, the recesses of Zaphon, and the divine title Most High. Apparently these verses allude to a mythological story about a minor god (Helel son of Shachar) who tried to take over Zaphon, the mountain of the gods. His attempted coup failed, and he was hurled down to the underworld. The king of Babylon is taunted for having similar unrealized delusions of grandeur. Some Christians have seen an allusion to the fall of Satan here, but this seems contextually unwarranted (see J. Martin, “Isaiah,” BKCOT, 1061).
Some understand the verb חָלַשׁ (khalash) to mean “weaken,” but HALOT 324 s.v. II חלשׁ proposes a homonym here meaning “defeat.”

In this line the taunting kings hint at the literal identity of the king, after likening him to the god Helel and a tree. The verb גָדַע (gadaʿ, “cut down”) is used of chopping down trees in 9:10 and 10:33.
verses.commentary:
14:12 "How you have fallen from heaven" The VERB (BDB 656, KB 709, Qal
PERFECT) denotes a settled condition. The question is, "Is this literal or figurative?" The
VERB is used for a violent death (BDB 657, Isa. 14:2a). Isaiah uses it in Isa. 3:8; 8:15 for
the destruction of a city. But the added phrase, "from heaven," is what causes commentators to assert an
angelic being, as well as the similar words of Jesus in Luke 10:18.

NASB
"O star of the morning"

NKJV, Vulgate
"O Lucifer"

NRSV
"O Day Star"

TEV
"bright morning star"

NJB, LXX
"Day star"

REB
"Bright morning star"

JPSOA, NET
"O Shining One"

Peshitta
"O Reviler of the nations"

The Hebrew NOMINATIVE MASCULINE term is
הילל (BDB 237, KB 245). This form is found
only here in the OT. The VERBAL root,
הלל can mean

- "shine," possibly referring to the new moon

- "be boastful" or "to praise," from which we get the Hallel psalms (i.e. praise psalms)

The KB mentions several options as to the origin of this root.

- from a Ugaritic root, hll

- from an Arabic root, the crescent of the new moon

- from a Hebrew root, uncertain, but probably refers to Venus the morning star ("son of the dawn")

- from the Latin, Lucifer referring to Venus (i.e. lit. "light-bearer")

The whole point of the title is that this heavenly light is quickly eclipsed by the morning light.
Its splendor is brief! There is a new, brighter, and better light coming!

▣ "You" The next two lines of Isa. 14:12 obviously refer to an earthly king of Assyria or
Babylon (cf. Isa. 14:16-17). The imagery of the poem (Isa. 14:4-21) is taken from Canaanite mythology
(esp. Isa. 14:13-14), which is known from Ras Shamra Tablets dating from the fifteenth
century B.C. found at the city of Ugarit.

The terms "star of the morning" (Helal) and "dawn" (Shabar) are both the
names of deities in Canaanite mythology, as is a mountain of the gods in the north (Mount Zaphon,
cf. Ps. 48:2). Also the title for deity, "Most High," is common in Ugaritic poems and refers
to Ba'al Shamim ("Lord of heaven"). In Canaanite mytho-poetry Helal, a lesser god, tries
to usurp power, but is defeated. This is behind Isaiah's imagery of an arrogant eastern potentate.

This description of a proud, arrogant Near Eastern king is extended from Isa. 14:8-11. Only
Isa. 14:12, taken literally following the Vulgate, and a lack of knowledge of Ugaritic literature can use
this context as referring to a rebellious angelic leader (i.e. Satan).

verses.zh: 你心里曾说：我要升到天上；我要高举我的宝座在　神众星以上；我要坐在聚会的山上，在北方的极处。
verses.en: You said to yourself,[NOTE:1] ‘I will climb up to the sky.Above the stars of El[NOTE:2] I will set up my throne.I will rule on the mountain of assemblyon the remote slopes of Zaphon.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “you, you said in your heart.”
In Canaanite mythology the stars of El were astral deities under the authority of the high god El.
Zaphon, the Canaanite version of Olympus, was the “mountain of assembly” where the gods met.
verses.commentary:
14:13-14 These two verses show the arrogance and pride of the ANE kings (see

SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP).

- "I will ascend to. . .," BDB 748, KB 828, Qal IMPERFECT

- "I will raise my throne. . .," BDB 926, KB 1202, Hiphil IMPERFECT

- "I will sit on. . .," BDB 442, KB 444, Qal IMPERFECT

- "I will ascend above...," same VERB as #1

- "I will make myself like. . .," BDB 197, KB 225, Hiphil IMPERFECT

Arrogance and pride are the essence of the fallen human spirit. YHWH uniquely judges this human
self-deification!

14:13 "stars of God" The title for Deity is El,
אל (BDB 42), which was a common designation of deity
throughout the ANE. This, too, could reflect the Canaanite mythology from Ugarit. See
G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible, "The Langauge of Myth," pp. 219, 242.

The stars were viewed as angels/gods who controlled human destiny
(i.e. Babylonian astral worship from Ziggurats). This person wanted total control over the earth.

▣ "I will sit on the mount of assembly

In the recesses of the north This is a Babylonian and Canaanite symbol of deity's abode (cf. Ps. 48:2;
Ezek. 28:14). The surprising thing is its location "in the recesses of the north." This mountain of the gods
in the far north was part of Canaanite mythology (i.e. Mt. Saphon). See Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, p. 279.
The Greek gods also lived on a mountain, Mount Olympus.

Remember, verses 13-14 are alleged statements of an ANE king.

verses.zh: 我要升到高云之上；我要与至上者同等。
verses.en: I will climb up to the tops[NOTE:1] of the clouds;I will make myself like the Most High!’[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “the high places.” This word often refers to the high places where pagan worship was conducted, but here it probably refers to the “backs” or tops of the clouds. See HALOT 136 s.v. בָּמָה.
Normally in the OT the title “Most High” belongs to the God of Israel, but in this context, where the mythological overtones are so strong, it probably refers to the Canaanite high god El.
verses.commentary:
14:14 "Most High" This title Elyon,
עליון (BDB 751 II; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, B.), is used by

- Balaam in Num. 24:16 and is parallel to Shaddai (i.e. Almighty, BDB 994; see

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI)

- Moses in his Song before his death in Deut. 32:8

- David in 2 Sam. 22:14 and in several Psalms

- in the Ras Shamra Tablets for the Canaanite High god

verses.zh: 然而，你必坠落阴间，到坑中极深之处。
verses.en: But you were brought down[NOTE:1] to Sheol,to the remote slopes of the Pit.[NOTE:2]
notes: The prefixed verb form is taken as a preterite. Note the use of perfects in v. 12 to describe the king’s downfall.
The Hebrew term בּוּר (bor, “cistern”) is sometimes used metaphorically to refer to the place of the dead or the entrance to the underworld.
verses.commentary:
14:15 Instead of going to the mountain in the far (BDB 438) north, he will go down to the depths
(BDB 438), Sheol.

The term Sheol (BDB 982, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?, I. B.) is parallel to "the pit" (BDB 92, cf. Ezek. 31:16),
which is another name for the grave (cf. Prov. 28:17). The same term is used in Isa. 14:19 and is parallel
to tomb/sepulcher (cf. Isa. 14:18).

The JPSOA translation's footnote (p. 813) asserts that "to the recesses of the pit" (NASB)
should be translated "to the bottom of the Pit." It bases this on Ezek. 32:21-32, where the lowest part of Sheol
is reserved for those who did not receive a proper burial (cf. Isa. 14:19).

verses.zh: 凡看见你的都要定睛看你，留意看你，说：使大地战抖，使列国震动，
verses.en: Those who see you stare at you,they look at you carefully, thinking:[NOTE:1] ‘Is this the man who shook the earth,the one who made kingdoms tremble?
notes: The word “thinking” is supplied in the translation in order to make it clear that the next line records their thoughts as they gaze at him.
verses.commentary:
14:16-19 This is the fourth strophe; it refers to the astonishment of the on-lookers in Sheol
at the body of the dead King of Babylon. It is similar to Isa. 14:9-11.

verses.zh: 使世界如同荒野，使城邑倾覆，不释放被掳的人归家，是这个人吗？
verses.en: Is this the one who made the world like a wilderness,who ruined its[NOTE:1] citiesand refused to free his prisoners so they could return home?’[NOTE:2]
notes: The pronominal suffix is masculine, even though its antecedent appears to be the grammatically feminine noun “world.” Some have suggested that the form עָרָיו (ʿarayv, plural noun with third masculine singular suffix) should be emended to עָרֶיהָ (ʿareha, plural noun with third feminine singular suffix). This emendation may be unnecessary in light of other examples of lack of agreement between a suffix and its antecedent noun.
Heb “and his prisoners did not let loose to [their] homes.” This really means, “he did not let loose his prisoners and send them back to their homes.” On the elliptical style, see GKC 366 §117.o.
verses.commentary:
14:17 This verse denotes the aggressive deportation practices of both Assyria and Babylon. This
population control mechanism is reversed by Cyrus II (Medo-Persia) in 538 B.C.

verses.zh: 列国的君王俱各在自己阴宅的荣耀中安睡。
verses.en: [NOTE:1] As for all the kings of the nations,all of them[NOTE:2] lie down in splendor,[NOTE:3] each in his own tomb.[NOTE:4]
notes: It is unclear where the quotation of the kings, begun in v. 10b, ends. However, the reference to the “kings of the nations” in v. 18 (see also v. 9) seems to indicate that the quotation has ended at this point and that Israel’s direct taunt (cf. vv. 4b-10a) has resumed. In fact, the references to the “kings of the nations” may form a stylistic inclusio or frame around the quotation.
The phrase “all of them” does not appear in the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa.
This refers to the typically extravagant burial of kings.
Heb “house” (so KJV, ASV), but in this context a tomb is in view. Note the verb “lie down” in the preceding line and the reference to a “grave” in the next line.

verses.zh: 惟独你被抛弃，不得入你的坟墓，好像可憎的枝子，以被杀的人为衣，就是被刀刺透，坠落坑中石头那里的；你又像被践踏的尸首一样。
verses.en: But you have been thrown out of your gravelike a shoot that is thrown away.[NOTE:1] You lie among[NOTE:2] the slain,among those who have been slashed by the sword,among those headed for[NOTE:3] the stones of the Pit,[NOTE:4] as if you were a mangled corpse.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “like a shoot that is abhorred.” The simile seems a bit odd; apparently it refers to a small shoot that is trimmed from a plant and tossed away. Some prefer to emend נֵצֶר (netser, “shoot”); some propose נֵפֶל (nefel, “miscarriage”). In this case one might paraphrase: “like a horrible-looking fetus that is delivered when a woman miscarries.”
Heb “are clothed with.”
Heb “those going down to.”
בּוֹר (bor) literally means “cistern”; cisterns were constructed from stones. On the metaphorical use of “cistern” for the underworld, see the note at v. 15.
Heb “like a trampled corpse.” Some take this line with what follows.
verses.commentary:
14:19

NASB
"like a rejected branch"

NASB margin
"like an abhorred branch"

NKJV
"like an abominable branch"

NRSV, REB, JPSOA
"like loathsome carrion"

NJB
"like a loathsome branch"

LXX
"like an abominable corpse"

Peshitta
"like an abominable person"

RSV, NEB
"like one untimely born"

NET
"like a shoot that is thrown away"

The MT has the NOUN "shoot" (BDB 666, KB 718 II), which the
Aramaic Targums translated as "miscarriage" (BDB 664, RSV, "an untimely birth).

This is followed by "loathed" (BDB 1073, KB 1765, Niphal
ACTIVE PARTICIPLE). This imagery refers to a rejected king as cast from his tomb.

The UBS Text Project, p. 31, gives "like a shoot" a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

This same term (BDB 666) is used in Isa. 6:13 of "the holy seed in the stump" and in Isa. 11:1
of the stem/shoot from Jesse, both of which refer to the Messiah, the true King. The kings of ANE are
a "rejected branch"!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BRANCH OF THE LORD

▣ "Like a trampled corpse" This speaks of the humiliation of an improper burial (possible
reference to Sargon II). Not only did the king miss the royal funeral, he missed burial altogether!

The term "trampled" (BDB 100, KB 115, Hophal PARTICIPLE) is
also used in Isa. 14:25 (Qal IMPERFECT).

- It was imagery for YHWH's judgment (cf. Isa. 63:6, Qal IMPERFECT
and 63:18, Polel PERFECT).

- The Psalms use it regularly for the covenant people's victory over enemies through YHWH's power
and presence (cf. Ps. 44:5; 60:12; 108:13).

- A disobedient covenant people trample God's land (cf. Jer. 12:10; Polel
PERFECT).

verses.zh: 你不得与君王同葬；因为你败坏你的国，杀戮你的民。恶人后裔的名，必永不提说。
verses.en: You will not be buried with them,[NOTE:1] because you destroyed your landand killed your people.“The offspring of the wickedwill never be mentioned again.
notes: Heb “you will not be united with them in burial” (so NASB).
verses.commentary:
14:20 Not only will the arrogant king be denied a proper burial, he will not be succeeded by a family
member. He and his family will be cut off. His own country will not remember him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

verses.zh: 先人既有罪孽，就要预备杀戮他的子孙，免得他们兴起来，得了遍地，在世上修满城邑。
verses.en: Prepare to execute[NOTE:1] his sonsfor the sins their ancestors have committed.[NOTE:2] They must not rise up and take possession of the earthor fill the surface of the world with cities.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “the place of slaughter for.”
Heb “for the sin of their fathers.”
J. N. Oswalt (Isaiah [NICOT], 1:320, n. 10) suggests that the garrison cities of the mighty empire are in view here.
verses.commentary:
14:21 The king's descendants will be killed because of their father's sins. This reflects Exod. 20:5.
The king and his wicked nation must not be allowed to prosper. YHWH wants the earth full, but not of
unrighteousness.

▣ "with cities" This line of poetry is a rejection of the Assyrian King's attempt to dominate
all of the ANE.

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华说：我必兴起攻击他们，将巴比伦的名号和所余剩的人，连子带孙一并剪除。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: “I will rise up against them,”says the Lord of Heaven’s Armies.“I will blot out all remembrance of Babylon and destroy all her people,[NOTE:1] including the offspring she produces,”[NOTE:2] says the Lord.
notes: Heb “I will cut off from Babylon name and remnant” (ASV, NAB, and NRSV all similar).
Heb “descendant and child.”
verses.commentary:
14:22-23 This forms a prose conclusion. It seems to me that Isa. 14:23 is related to Isa. 13:21-22,
which is imagery to describe the total desolation of this nation, this king, and his city.

14:22 "offspring and posterity" These two terms refer to descendants.

- current children (BDB 630)

- the family tree or lineage (BDB 645)

Loss of descendants was seen as a great shame and curse in the ANE (cf. Isa. 47:9). It may
even have been thought to affect one's afterlife.

verses.zh: 我必使巴比伦为箭猪所得，又变为水池；我要用灭亡的扫帚扫净它。这是万军之耶和华说的。
verses.en: “I will turn her into a place that is overrun with wild animals[NOTE:1] and covered with pools of stagnant water.I will get rid of her, just as one sweeps away dirt with a broom,”[NOTE:2] says the Lord of Heaven’s Armies.
notes: Heb “I will make her into a possession of wild animals.” It is uncertain what type of animal קִפֹּד (qippod) refers to. Some suggest a rodent (cf. NASB, NRSV “hedgehog”), others, an owl (cf, NAB, NIV, TEV).
Heb “I will sweep her away with the broom of destruction.”
verses.commentary:
14:23 "I will sweep it with the broom of destruction" YHWH is depicted as a wife/child cleaning the house
by sweeping (BDB 370, KB 367, Pilpel PERFECT with waw). All the trash
is removed. What a domestic, but powerful imagery (unique to Isaiah).

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华起誓说：我怎样思想，必照样成就；我怎样定意，必照样成立，
verses.en: [NOTE:1] The Lord of Heaven’s Armies makes this solemn vow:“Be sure of this:Just as I have intended, so it will be;just as I have planned, it will happen.
notes: Having announced the downfall of the Chaldean empire, the Lord appends to this prophecy a solemn reminder that the Assyrians, the major Mesopotamian power of Isaiah’s day, would be annihilated, foreshadowing what would subsequently happen to Babylon and the other hostile nations.
verses.commentary:
14:24-27 Most English translations make a paragraph change here. But notice there is no "oracle" marker,
which implies that Isa. 13:1-14:27 is one literary unit dealing with the destruction of Assyria. See Contextual
Insights, C.

There is only one causality in OT theology—YHWH (cf. 2 Chr. 20:6; Eccl. 7:14; Isa. 14:24-27;
43:13; 45:7; 54:16; Jer. 18:11; Lam. 3:33-38; Amos 3:6b). It is a literary and theological way to assert YHWH's sovereignty!
The OT does not discuss secondary causes.

- angelic temptation

- human choices

- natural calamities

- diseases

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

14:24 This verse asserts that God's plans and purposes will be accomplished. His word is sure (cf.
Isa. 46:11; 55:8-9; Job 23:13; Ps. 33:9; Acts 4:28).

▣ "The Lord of hosts has sworn" By the power and authority of Himself,
YHWH states His plans and purposes (cf. Isa. 14:24; 45:23; 62:8; Deut. 1:8,35; 2:14; 4:31; 6:10,18,23; Jer. 51:14;
Amos 4:2; 8:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LORD OF HOSTS

verses.zh: 就是在我地上打折亚述人，在我山上将他践踏。他加的轭必离开以色列人；他加的重担必离开他们的肩头。
verses.en: I will break Assyria[NOTE:1] in my land,I will trample them[NOTE:2] underfoot on my hills.Their yoke will be removed from my people,the burden will be lifted from their shoulders.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “to break Assyria.”
Heb “him.” This is a collective singular referring to the nation, or a reference to the king of Assyria, who by metonymy stands for the entire nation.

Heb “and his [i.e., Assyria’s] yoke will be removed from them [the people?], and his [Assyria’s] burden from his [the nation’s?] shoulder will be removed.” There are no antecedents in this oracle for the suffixes in the phrases “from them” and “from his shoulder.” Since the Lord’s land and hills are referred to in the preceding line and the statement seems to echo 10:27, it is likely that God’s people are the referents of the suffixes; the translation uses “my people” to indicate this.
verses.commentary:
14:25 "to break Assyria in My land" This may refer to the plague which devastated 185,000 troops of
Sennacherib in one night before the gates of Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day (cf. 2 Kgs. 18:13-19:37,
esp. 19:35-37; 2 Chronicles 32).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN

▣ "his yoke will be removed from them" This is a recurrent theme (cf. Isa. 9:4; 10:27). Yoke,
like "staff" or "rod," was imagery of foreign oppression.

verses.zh: 这是向全地所定的旨意；这是向万国所伸出的手。
verses.en: This is the plan I have devised for the whole earth;my hand is ready to strike all the nations.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and this is the hand that is outstretched over all the nations.”
verses.commentary:
14:26-27 This Assyrian king had a plan for world domination (Isa. 14:26), but YHWH had another plan
(cf. Isa. 8:10), a plan for world redemption (Isa. 14:27)! Assyria, Babylon and Persia are tools in YHWH's
plan and no one can withstand His hand.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

verses.zh: 万军之耶和华既然定意，谁能废弃呢？他的手已经伸出，谁能转回呢？
verses.en: Indeed,[NOTE:1] the Lord of Heaven’s Armies has a plan,and who can possibly frustrate it?His hand is ready to strike,and who can possibly stop it?[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “For” (KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV).
Heb “His hand is outstretched, and who will turn it back?”

verses.zh: 亚哈斯王崩的那年，就有以下的默示：
verses.en: This oracle[NOTE:1] came in the year that King Ahaz died:[NOTE:2]
notes: See note at Isa 13:1.
Perhaps 715 b.c., but the precise date is uncertain.
verses.commentary:
14:28 Notice there is an "oracle" mentioned in Isa. 14:28-32 which deals with YHWH's judgment on
Philistia (i.e. the Philistines), but this is not linked to the Assyrian-oriented strophe of Isa. 14:24-27.

This strophe (vv. 28-32) is a separate prophecy about YHWH's judgment of Philistia. It is not
related to the oracle about Assyria in vv. 1-23.

▣ "In the year that King Ahaz died" In my OT
SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF THE DIVIDED MONARCHY,
three scholars give their proposed dates for Ahaz.

- John Bright, 735 ‒ 715 B.C.

- E. J. Young, 736 ‒ 728 B.C.

- R. K Harrison, 732/731 ‒ 716/715 B.C.

These dates (reign and co-reign, not necessarily death) could fit four aggressive Assyrian kings.

- Tiglath-Pileser III, 745 ‒ 727 B.C.

- Shalmaneser V, 727 ‒ 722 B.C.

- Sargon II, 722 ‒ 705 B.C.

- Sennacherib, 705 ‒ 681 B.C. (185,000 soldiers killed before the walls
of Jerusalem in 701 B.C., cf. Isaiah 36-39; 2 Kings 18-19).

Number 3, Sargon II, died in battle away from home and did participate in a military campaign
against Philistia.

verses.zh: 非利士全地啊，不要因击打你的杖折断就喜乐。因为从蛇的根必生出毒蛇；它所生的是火焰的飞龙。
verses.en: Don’t be so happy, all you Philistines,just because the club that beat you[NOTE:1] has been broken![NOTE:2] For a viper will grow out of the serpent’s root,and its fruit will be a darting adder.[NOTE:3]
notes: The identity of this “club” (also referred to as a “serpent” in the next line) is uncertain. It may refer to an Assyrian king, or to Ahaz. For discussion see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:331-32. The viper/adder referred to in the second half of the verse is his successor.

Heb “flying burning one.” The designation “burning one” may allude to the serpent’s appearance or the effect of its poisonous bite. (See the note at 6:2.) The qualifier “flying” probably refers to the serpent’s quick, darting movements, though one might propose a homonym here, meaning “biting.” (See J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah [NICOT], 1:332, n. 18.) Some might think in terms of a mythological flying, fire-breathing dragon (cf. NAB “a flying saraph”; CEV “a flying fiery dragon”), but this proposal does not make good sense in 30:6, where the phrase “flying burning one” appears again in a list of desert animals.

The Hebrew text has, “the firstborn of the poor will graze.” “Firstborn” may be used here in an idiomatic sense to indicate the very poorest of the poor. See BDB 114 s.v. בְּכוֹר. The translation above assumes an emendation of בְּכוֹרֵי (bekhore, “firstborn of”) to בְּכָרַי (bekharay, “in my pastures”).
verses.commentary:
14:29 Philistia is commanded not to rejoice (BDB 970, KB 1333, Qal IMPERFECT
used in a JUSSIVE sense) because the evil empire has been defeated. Their
short-term deliverance will not last!

▣ The last two lines of Isa. 14:29 are very ambiguous and uncertain. They seem to mean that things
will go from bad to worse.

The phrase "flying serpent" is the NOUN "serpent" (BDB 977 I,
cf. Isa. 30:6; Num. 21:6) plus the PARTICIPLE "flying" (BDB 733, KB 800, Polel
PARTICIPLE), which denotes rapid movement (i.e. striking, sliding, darting).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERAPHIM

verses.zh: 贫寒人的长子必有所食；穷乏人必安然躺卧。我必以饥荒治死你的根；你所余剩的人必被杀戮。
verses.en: The poor will graze in my pastures;[NOTE:1] the needy will rest securely.But I will kill your root by famine;it will put to death all your survivors.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “your remnant” (so NAB, NRSV).
Or “despair” (see HALOT 555 s.v. מוג). The form נָמוֹג (namog) should be taken here as an infinitive absolute functioning as an imperative. See GKC 199-200 §72.v.
verses.commentary:
14:30 The first two lines refer to God's care for

- His covenant people who have been oppressed by Philistia (cf. Isa. 14:32c) or

- the needy of society; the MT uses the imagery "the first-born of the poor"

▣ "I will destroy. . .it will kill" These two lines of poetry describe YHWH's action "I," v. 30c, by the
means of famine, the "it" of v. 30d. This is another example of OT theology whereby there are no secondary causes,
only God's actions.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

verses.zh: 门哪，应当哀号！城啊，应当呼喊！非利士全地啊，你都消化了！因为有烟从北方出来，他行伍中并无乱队的。
verses.en: Wail, O city gate!Cry out, O city!Melt with fear,[NOTE:1] all you Philistines!For out of the north comes a cloud of smoke,and there are no stragglers in its ranks.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and there is no one going alone in his appointed places.” The meaning of this line is uncertain. בּוֹדֵד (boded) appears to be a participle from בָּדַד (badad, “be separate”; see BDB 94 s.v. בָּדַד). מוֹעָד (moʿad) may mean “assembly” or, by extension, “multitude” (see HALOT 558 s.v. *מוֹעָד), but the referent of the third masculine pronominal suffix attached to the noun is unclear. It probably refers to the “nation” mentioned in the next line.
The question forces the Philistines to consider the dilemma they will face—surrender and oppression, or battle and death.
verses.commentary:
14:31 "Wail, O gate; cry, O city" These two IMPERATIVES

- wail, BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil

- cry, BDB 277, KB 277, Qal

describe the overthrow of the five cities of the Philistines, each with its own king (city states).

▣ "Melt away, O Philistia, all of you" The VERB (BDB 556,
KB 555, Niphal INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) describes the paralyzing fear
which grips a population (cf. Exod. 15:15; Josh. 2:9,24; 1 Sam. 14:16).

Note this phrase refers to the destruction of the entire society (cf. Jeremiah 47 and Amos 1:6-8).

14:31 "For smoke comes from the north" The empires of the Fertile Crescent are to the east of Canaan,
but because of the desert in between their armies, had to follow the Euphrates to its headwaters and then
move south along the coastal plain. Therefore, "north" became an idiom of invasion, evil, and destruction.

- here it refers to Assyria

- in Jer. 4:6; 6:1,22; 10:22; 13:20; 15:12; 46:20,24; Ezek. 26:7 it refers to Neo-Babylon

▣ "there is no straggler in his ranks" This describes a new Mesopotamian invader. One is gone
(cf. Isa. 14:29), but another one, a worse one (cf. Isa. 14:29c,d), is coming!

verses.zh: 可怎样回答外邦（或指非利士）的使者呢？必说：耶和华建立了锡安；他百姓中的困苦人必投奔在其中。
verses.en: How will they respond to the messengers of this nation?[NOTE:1] Indeed, the Lord has made Zion secure;the oppressed among his people will find safety in her.
verses.commentary:
14:32 "seek refuge" See SPECIAL TOPIC: REFUGE (OT)

"Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- There has been much discussion on the relationship of Isa. 14:12-21 to Satan. It seems
to me that we must take seriously the historical context and specific literary statements of
Isaiah and assert that originally this referred to the king of old Babylon (or kings of Assyria
after Ashurbanipal). However, the king of old Babylon's problem, as all conscious creatures,
was pride. If we go back to Gen. 3:5, we see this desire to be like God. Not only has sin affected
the angelic world, but also the material world (cf. Daniel 4; 11:36; Ezek. 28:13ff; 2 Thess. 2:4). The
king is a type of wicked leadership. Behind the wicked world leaders in the OT stood their national
deities (cf. Dan. 10:13,20; also note Deut. 32:8 in the LXX). From the NT we understand that there
is a personal force of evil known as Satan. The identification in this chapter with Satan was
probably influenced by

- Jerome's Vulgate translating Isa. 14:12 as "Lucifer"

- Tertulian and Gregory the Great relating this passage to Luke 10:18

- This passage being used as a backdrop to both Dante's Inferno and Milton's
Paradise Lost

SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN

- I personally am feeling more and more uncomfortable using Isaiah 14 and Ezekiel 28 as biblical
texts for the origin and demise of an angelic tempter. I think our curiosity drives us to use contexts
inappropriately. The Bible is silent on many issues that we are curious about. Systematic Theology
must start with exegesis! In many ways the spiritual realm is purposefully clouded and concealed.

- For a similar context see Ezekiel 28 at
www.freebiblecommentary.org,
"Old Testament Studies," written commentaries.

- The Jewish Study Bible (p. 812) says of this poem "it describes the ignominious death of an
Assyrian monarch of Isaiah's time, probably Sargon II, who was killed in battle in 705 B.C.
It was later reinterpreted as predicting the death of a Babylonian monarch." I think Isaiah (or a disciple)
may have used an earlier poem, or at least its imagery, to describe a series of arrogant eastern kings
who were destroyed by YHWH.

- It is impossible to fit together all the historical allusions in this prophecy. Remember, Hebrew
prophecy is a historical "pointer," not a detailed road map. Westerners misunderstand the OT's
imagery, ambiguity, and hyperbole! See D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking
the Language of Biblical Prophecy and Apocalyptic and G. B. Caird, The Language and
Imagery of the Bible. Both books have been very helpful to me on this issue.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 14:1-2

1When the Lord will have compassion on
Jacob and again choose Israel, and settle them in their own land, then strangers will join them and attach themselves to the
house of Jacob. 2The peoples will take them along and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel will
possess them as an inheritance in the land of the Lord as male servants and female servants;
and they will take their captors captive and will rule over their oppressors.
